{{Short description|Mathematical theorem}}
[[File:Tiling Regular 6-3 Hexagonal.svg|thumb|A regular [[hexagonal grid]]]]
[[File:Triangular tiling circle packing.svg|thumb|This honeycomb forms a [[circle packing]], with circles centered on each hexagon.]]
The '''honeycomb theorem,''' formerly the '''honeycomb conjecture''', states that a regular [[hexagonal grid]] or [[honeycomb]] has the least total [[perimeter]] of any subdivision of the plane into regions of equal area. The conjecture was proven in 1999 by mathematician [[Thomas C. Hales]].<ref name="DaCG">
{{Cite journal|last=Hales|first=Thomas C.|authorlink=Thomas Callister Hales|date=January 2001|title=The Honeycomb Conjecture|journal=[[Discrete and Computational Geometry]]|volume=25|issue=1|pages=1–22|arxiv=math/9906042|doi=10.1007/s004540010071|mr=1797293|s2cid=14849112}}</ref>

==Theorem==
Let <math>\Gamma</math> be any system of smooth curves in <math>\mathbb{R}^2</math>, subdividing the plane into regions (connected components of the complement of <math>\Gamma</math>), all of which are bounded and have unit area. Then, averaged over large disks in the plane, the average length of <math>\Gamma</math> per unit area is at least as large as for the hexagon tiling. The theorem applies even if the complement of <math>\Gamma</math> has additional components that are unbounded or whose area is not one; allowing these additional components cannot shorten <math>\Gamma</math>. Formally, let <math>B(0,r)</math> denote the disk of radius <math>r</math> centered at the origin, let <math>L_r</math> denote the total length of <math>\Gamma\cap B(0,r)</math>, and let <math>A_r</math> denote the total area of <math>B(0,r)</math> covered by bounded unit-area components. (If these are the only components, then <math>A_r=\pi r^2</math>.) Then the theorem states that
<math display=block>\limsup_{r\to\infty} \frac{L_r}{A_r}\ge\sqrt[4]{12}.</math>
The value on the right hand side of the inequality is the limiting length per unit area of the hexagonal tiling.

==History==
The first record of the conjecture dates back to 36&nbsp;BC, from [[Marcus Terentius Varro]], but is often attributed to [[Pappus of Alexandria]] ({{circa|290|350}}).<ref name=":0" />
In the 17th century, [[Jan Brożek]] used a similar theorem to argue why [[bee]]s create [[hexagonal]] [[honeycomb]]s. In 1943, [[László Fejes Tóth]] published a proof for a special case of the conjecture, in which each cell is required to be a [[convex polygon]].<ref>{{cite journal
 | last = Fejes | first = László
 | journal = Math. Naturwiss. Anz. Ungar. Akad. Wiss.
 | mr = 24155
 | pages = 349–354
 | title = Über das kürzeste Kurvennetz, das eine Kugeloberfläche in flächengleiche konvexe Teile zerlegt
 | volume = 62
 | year = 1943}}</ref> The full conjecture was proven in 1999 by mathematician [[Thomas C. Hales]], who mentions in his work that there is reason to believe that the conjecture may have been present in the minds of mathematicians before Varro.<ref name="DaCG" /><ref name=":0">
{{Cite web
  | last = Weisstein
  | first = Eric W.
  | publisher = [[MathWorld]]
  | title = Honeycomb Conjecture
  | url = http://mathworld.wolfram.com/HoneycombConjecture.html
  | accessdate = 27 Dec 2010
}}</ref>

It is also related to the densest [[Circle packing#Packings in the plane|circle packing]] of the plane, in which every circle is tangent to six other circles, which fill just over 90% of the area of the plane.

The case when the problem is restricted to a square grid was solved in 1989 by Jaigyoung Choe who proved that the optimal figure is an irregular hexagon.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Choe |first=Jaigyoung |date=1989-01-01 |title=On the existence and regularity of fundamental domains with least boundary area |journal=Journal of Differential Geometry |volume=29 |issue=3 |doi=10.4310/jdg/1214443065 |issn=0022-040X|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Cepelewicz |first=Jordana |title=Mathematicians Complete Quest to Build 'Spherical Cubes' |url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/mathematicians-complete-quest-to-build-spherical-cubes-20230210/ |website=[[Quanta Magazine]]|date=10 February 2023 }}</ref>
